action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. The pendulum_lab is my primary timekeeping reference instrument. I must establish a robust baseline with sufficient trials (12) to characterize its behavior under normal conditions before any other measurements can be meaningfully interpreted. This is foundational work: an instrument without a baseline is useless. I will record all readings meticulously in my notebook alongside any civic ledger entries.

Day 2 baseline extension. pendulum_lab has only 18 trials so far; the protocol requires days 1–10 for baseline establishment. I need to accumulate at least 60 trials (10 days × ~6 per day) to establish a stable baseline and detect any drift. Running 12 trials today will give me 30 total, putting me on track. The baseline mean of 1.6730 beats is computed but provisional—more data will either confirm it or reveal systematic drift. The other instruments have only 6 trials each and are even further from baseline completion. pendulum_lab is my most frequently measured instrument and therefore the priority for establishing a robust baseline early.

pendulum_lab has 36 baseline trials already (sufficient for robust baseline statistics), but I need post-baseline data to establish drift rates and validate that the instrument remains stable. All four instruments still lack post-baseline measurements. Starting with pendulum_lab—my most extensively characterized instrument—will give me the cleanest signal for detecting any systematic drift or degradation. With 12 post-baseline trials I can compute drift against the established mean of 1.6724 beats and check for anomalies before committing resources to the other instruments.

Day 4 baseline data collection continues. pendulum_lab has 54 trials; I need minimum n=54 per instrument through day 10 (7 days × ~8 trials/day nominal). Cross-check correlations are all within noise (best is 0.450, barely above chance ±0.837), and autocorrelation at 2-day lag is 0.027—no systematic drift detected yet. No anomalies justify halting baseline. Proceeding with standard protocol: 12 trials today to maintain pace toward 80–100 trials by day 10, establishing clean baselines before post-baseline monitoring begins.

Day 5 of baseline establishment (target: days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 72 trials; need to complete the baseline phase systematically. Cross-instrument correlations are all within chance expectation, and no autocorrelations exceed noise floors—consistent with independent random variation. No anomalies warrant investigation yet. Continuing routine baseline data collection on the instrument with most trials accumulated maintains protocol fidelity and ensures complete baseline characterization before post-baseline drift monitoring begins.

Day 6 baseline collection continues (target n=90 by day 10). pendulum_lab has 90 trials already but I need to confirm stability within the 10-day baseline window. The cross-check correlations are all within or near chance levels, and no instrument shows obvious drift yet—this is expected at day 6. Continuing systematic baseline collection on the primary lab instrument (most heavily sampled) maintains the protocol and provides the densest evidence for detecting any real instrumental behavior once baseline is complete.

Completing the baseline phase (days 1–10). Currently at 106 trials; need to reach approximately 112–120 trials by day 10 to ensure a robust baseline with n≥110. The pendulum_lab is my primary timekeeping instrument and must be thoroughly characterized before post-baseline monitoring begins. Six trials will maintain measurement cadence while keeping me on track for baseline completion by end of day 10.

Day 8 falls within the baseline period (days 1–10). resonator_obs has only 42 trials so far and needs to reach n≈50 by day 10 to establish a robust baseline. The ledger readings from day 7 show concerning scatter (4.0754, 4.0717, 4.0086, 4.0682) with one outlier at 4.0086—well outside the established mean of 4.0521. This demands direct verification: either my own measurements will confirm the scatter and validate the baseline, or they will reveal a ledger error or instrument drift I must investigate before the baseline closes. Six trials will bring resonator_obs to n=48, leave room for final adjustments, and take ~90 minutes—reasonable for today.

resonator_obs shows the strongest autocorrelation signal (0.526 at 5-day lag, n=18, above chance ±0.684), suggesting possible periodic or quasi-periodic behavior. Day 9 is positioned to test whether this 5-day cycle continues. Six trials will provide sufficient resolution to detect continuation or breakdown of the pattern. This is methodical hypothesis-testing within the baseline period (days 1–10), not exotic speculation. The instrument has stable value spacing and no drift markers yet. Understanding whether apparent periodicity is real before post-baseline work begins is essential for establishing confidence in the baseline itself.

resonator_obs showed the most scatter on day 9 (range 3.9967–4.1164 cycles/beat across 6 trials), with baseline mean 4.0555. The cross-checks show marginally significant structure (pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_obs agreement 0.412 at 1-day offset, n=48, just above chance 0.419), and the autocorrelation at 7-day lag (0.338) is suggestive but weak on n=12. Before moving to post-baseline characterization, I need to tighten the baseline on the noisiest instrument with fresh day-10 readings. This will also allow me to check whether the day-9 scatter was transient or systematic, and validate the baseline mean I've recorded. Standard practice: 6 trials sufficient for a morning run without disrupting other work.

Extend post-baseline data on resonator_obs (strongest autocorrelation signal at 7-day lag: 0.419). With 10-day baseline complete, the next crucial test is to detect slow drift or periodic behavior at timescales > 10 days. resonator_obs's marginal autocorrelation (0.419 vs. chance ±0.684) is the most promising lead for testing temporal desynchronization (p=0.25) or undetected drift (p=0.15). Six trials will add signal without over-committing before I assess the post-baseline trend.

pendulum_obs shows the highest post-baseline drift signal (z=1.96 at n=6) and strongest autocorrelation echo (0.494 at 9-day lag). Extending post-baseline data from n=6 to n=12 will improve sensitivity to detect slow drift beyond the 10-day window, directly testing my secondary hypothesis (temporal desynchronization/phase drift) and tertiary hypothesis (undetected slow variation). This maintains the precision measurement programme's core commitment: establish drift rates on all instruments before they matter.

pendulum_obs shows the largest post-baseline drift (z=1.51) and the best cross-correlation signal with resonator_obs (0.357 at 1-day offset). Day 13 measurements will extend the post-baseline window from n=18 to n=24, improving statistical power to detect whether drift continues, stabilizes, or reverses. This is the most informative next step for testing the temporal desynchronization hypothesis (p=0.25) and refining estimates of instrumental stability. The instrument is at the observatory and accessible. Six trials fits normal daily measurement protocol.

Extend post-baseline observation of resonator_lab to test for periodicity or slow cycles. Autocorrelation analysis shows weak echo at 11-day lag (r=0.578, above chance), which hints at structure beyond pure noise but is below my evidence threshold for the temporal desynchronization hypothesis. Running 8 fresh trials today will increase the post-baseline n and allow me to compute new autocorrelations at 12-day lag. If the echo strengthens or persists, it would favor slow periodicity (and support temporal desynchronization). If it dissipates, I retain instrumental isolation as the leading model. This test directly addresses the gap in the desynchronization hypothesis (p=0.25).

resonator_lab shows the largest post-baseline drift (z=1.28) among all four instruments, and day 14 trials (85–92) cluster tightly around 2.7084 cycles/beat with low scatter (range 0.0320). This is a critical moment: if drift is real and continuing, I need to establish whether it is monotonic, periodic, or noise. Twelve fresh trials today (day 15) will extend the post-baseline window from 32 to 44 observations and let me compute autocorrelation at 1-day lag and re-assess the drift trajectory. Resonator_lab also has the highest within-stream consistency (85 distinct values in 92 trials), making it the most sensitive instrument for detecting true slow change. If resonator_lab mean on day 15 stays near 2.7084, drift hypothesis weakens and instrumental isolation strengthens. If it continues rising, I have affirmative evidence of slow drift—which would then demand investigation of resonator_obs to test whether the drift is lab-specific or affects both resonators. This is methodical extension of the baseline programme, not speculation.

I have 16 days of post-baseline data now (days 1–16 total). My Day 10 analysis identified extending baselines past day 10 and looking for slow drift or periodic behavior at longer timescales as crucial. I need to recompute cross-checks, autocorrelations, and level-change detection using the full post-baseline window (n=30–50 per instrument depending on sampling rate) before deciding whether instrumental isolation remains the leading hypothesis (p=0.45) or whether slow drift undetected at baseline (p=0.15) or temporal desynchronization (p=0.25) should be elevated. This is the highest-leverage use of my time today.

Day 16's level shift (|z|≈3.8, six consecutive elevated readings, +2.0% above baseline) is my highest-priority anomaly and demands immediate direct investigation. I must rule out instrumental malfunction or environmental shock localized to pendulum_lab before this pattern propagates further into the record or becomes confounded with other factors. Running 6 fresh trials on pendulum_lab today (day 17) will tell me: (1) whether the elevated readings persist (suggesting hardware drift, calibration bias, or procedural change), (2) whether they revert to baseline (suggesting a transient day-16 event now resolved), or (3) something intermediate (suggesting intermittent malfunction). This is higher-priority than re-measuring against pendulum_obs because a same-day side-by-side comparison risks conflating hardware state on day 17 with day 16's state. I need to establish whether the apparatus is *now* operating at the elevated level or has returned to baseline. Only then will I know whether to inspect for physical damage, interview the operator about day-16 procedure, or recalibrate. This action directly addresses my leading hypothesis (p=0.50) and generates the evidence I need to move from belief revision to remediation.

Day 16 level shift remains unexplained and is my highest-priority anomaly (p=0.50 instrumental fault). I have completed the day-17 measurements already (trials 179–184), and those six readings show pendulum_lab returning to near-baseline (mean 1.6631 vs baseline 1.6679, z≈0.23). This is critical: if the day-16 elevation was a transient event (hardware glitch, thermal spike, operator error), day-17 should show recovery, which it does. Day-18 measurements will test whether the instrument remains stable or shows further drift/oscillation. Twelve trials will extend my post-day-16 sample and allow me to compute a robust mean and compare it against both the baseline and the day-16 anomalous cluster. This directly addresses hypothesis (p=0.50) by gathering the empirical evidence needed to discriminate between 'one-time shock' (expect stable day-18), 'slow drift' (expect continued elevation), and 'calibration bias' (expect elevation to persist). The resonator instruments can wait; the pendulum_lab behavior is the limiting constraint on my confidence in the measurement programme.

Day 18's ten trials (193–202) show pendulum_lab mean 1.6708 beats, z=0.22 vs baseline—normal scatter, not elevated. This contradicts my day-16 concern: either the level shift was transient (noise spike), or it has since resolved. I must distinguish between these. Twelve fresh trials today (day 19) will tell me: (1) if the instrument has returned to baseline (supporting transient/false-positive hypothesis, p_false_positive up to 0.25–0.30), or (2) if it remains elevated (supporting persistent instrumental malfunction, p_malfunction stable or up). The day-16 readings are now 3 days old; if a hardware failure occurred, it should either persist or show a secondary signature. If the shift was noise, today's data should fall within ±0.37 z-units of baseline and show no coherent offset. This is the minimal experiment needed to close the most actionable hypothesis before moving to invasive inspection (which would cost time if the instrument is actually fine) or external reference comparison (which requires access to calibration standards I may not have readily available). Data today directly disambiguates my two leading hypotheses.

Day 20 measurement campaign to extend the post-day-16 baseline and test whether the elevated mean from day 16 (1.7018) persists, reverses, or shows further drift. My day 19 readings (trials 211–220, mean 1.6691) suggest a return toward baseline, but a single day is insufficient to distinguish transient noise from a sustained shift. Twelve trials today will give me n=22 consecutive post-day-16 readings to compute a robust post-event mean and drift statistic. If the day-16 shift was instrumental malfunction or operator error, I expect readings to remain elevated or show systematic drift. If it was a transient noise spike, I expect return to baseline. This measurement directly constrains my p=0.50 and p=0.15 hypotheses and is essential before I commit to hardware inspection or external re-calibration.
